source.title: Low-Pass Filtering SGD for Recovering Flat Optima in the Deep Learning Optimization Landscape
source.authors: Devansh Bisla; Jing Wang; A. Choromańska

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extracting the relevant result.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports a training-accuracy threshold for CIFAR-10 ResNet18 models trained with SGD, but uses that threshold to select models for a sharpness/generalization analysis rather than to study training error itself.
record.gate_note: The authors say models were trained until cross-entropy reached ≈0.01, corresponding to ≈99% training accuracy, and models that did not reach that threshold were discarded. Their statement that large networks can easily achieve zero training error with data or label noise cites Zhang et al. (2016a) and is not this study's result. No separate training-error results are reported for the noise experiments.
record.test_reason: The study conditions its sharpness analysis on reaching cross-entropy ≈0.01 (described as ≈99% training accuracy), discarding failures without reporting their number or conditions. This is a selection criterion, not a test of V1. Its reported outcomes concern sharpness, generalization and optimizer performance; none directly test V2–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that LPF sharpness tracks generalization comparatively well and that LPF-SGD compares favorably with common training strategies. They do not conclude that gradient training generally reaches near-zero training classification error.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses momentum SGD on CIFAR-10 ResNet18 models and selects models that meet a ≈99% training-accuracy threshold; it does not report training-error outcomes as the target finding.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors discard models that do not reach the cross-entropy threshold, so the reported sharpness analysis is conditional on reaching approximately 99% training accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: LPF sharpness correlates with generalization gap overall (Kendall correlation 0.606±0.03), with negative correlations when varying width or batch normalization (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpness measures differ in how well they track generalization, depending on the architectural or optimizer parameter varied.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimizer comparisons report validation error, BLEU scores and computational cost; the width experiment reports validation double descent and sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LPF-based optimization can improve generalization relative to the tested optimizers, and LPF sharpness can track validation double descent.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The training-accuracy threshold is a selection criterion, not a reported distribution of outcomes; models that failed to reach it were excluded, and the number excluded is not stated. The cited claim about fitting noisy labels is prior work, not a result of this study.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the ≈99% training-accuracy threshold is a selection criterion and the paper does not report it as an outcome for the full set of models. Noise-related training-error claims in Section 3.2 are cited prior work or are not reported as training-error outcomes.

untested.parts: Training classification-error outcomes across the attempted models, including excluded runs; fitting corrupted or random labels; CIFAR-100 training error; and effects of model size, stopping and regularization on training error. Section 11.4 uses Adam and 20% label noise but reports validation error and sharpness.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious-minimum frequencies and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts or special initialization.
Initialization-dependent learning speed, signal propagation and trainable depth.
Loss and curvature trajectories relative to the learning-rate stability threshold, recovery and divergence.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and tolerated learning rates, and comparison with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Keep the ≈99% threshold out of outcome rows, as rows_left_out already specifies. The noisy-label zero-training-error statement in Section 3.2 cites prior work. Table 9 is internally inconsistent: its surrounding text calls the values training cross-entropy, whereas its caption calls them validation loss. It compares losses before and after network balancing and supplies no unambiguous training classification-error result. Varying batch normalization or shortcuts in sharpness correlations does not measure training acceleration or depth degradation.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports only the ≈99% training-accuracy selection threshold, not model-specific outcomes or how many of the 2916 models failed it. It does not report zero or near-zero training error for corrupted or random labels as its own result. CIFAR-100, Adam, smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes are not tested for this version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
